judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2764. It cuts the state income tax and sets a path to cut it again. The act rewrites the income tax table from the 2026 tax year. Six brackets become four. The top rate falls from 4.75 percent to 4.5 percent. The first $3,750 of taxable income is taxed at nothing, or $7,500 for a couple filing together. The act then sets a trigger for further cuts. Each February the State Board of Equalization weighs tax collections against a base year. If they have grown past a set threshold, every rate falls by another quarter of a percentage point. That can repeat until the rates reach zero. If the state declares a revenue failure, the cut waits for a later reading of the figures. The Oklahoma House passed it 74-19. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 460. It makes natural gas the state's preferred fuel for new power plants. Oklahoma law already named natural gas the preferred choice for new fossil fuel power plants. That preference ran out at the start of 2020. The act brings it back with no end date. It also widens it. The preference now covers every new power plant, not only the ones that burn fossil fuel, and any added capacity at a plant already running. A company that picks another fuel may put evidence to the Corporation Commission, which sets electric rates, that its choice is better for customers. The act took effect as soon as it was signed. The Oklahoma House passed it 70-19. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 758. It limits how many days of online lessons a school may count as class time. Oklahoma schools must hold 180 days of classroom instruction, or 1,080 hours. From the 2026-2027 school year, a day when school is shut and lessons go online no longer counts toward that total. One narrow exception is left. A district may count up to two such days, or twelve hours, but only if three things line up. The state superintendent must have approved the district's virtual plan. The Governor must have declared an emergency that bears on how schools run. And the local board must approve the closure. The plan must say how the district will teach students on a disability plan, feed students, and carry students to technology center courses. Full-time virtual schools are outside the rule. The state must report each year which districts shut and why. The Oklahoma House passed it 53-32. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 212. It sets up a two-year trial of new routes into teaching. The program is called TeachForwardOK. The Commission for Educational Quality and Accountability runs it. The commission hires outside experts to review teacher training at state colleges. A college program applies, and if it is approved it gets a grant to take part and to pay the reviewer. The review looks at how the program recruits trainees and how many finish, how well it prepares them, whether it meets the state's need for teachers, and how it might reach people who come by a less usual route. The program then has ninety days to say how it will act on what the review found. The act points to routes such as school aides training on the job to become teachers. One program is picked for $500,000 to carry out its plan, if the money is there. The commission reports to state leaders by the end of 2027. The Oklahoma House passed it 51-29. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1618. It makes a court use a risk report before setting release terms in a violent case. A public safety report is a risk assessment. A pretrial release program runs it. It predicts how likely a defendant is to miss court, or to be arrested again, while waiting for trial. The report may set out the person's past convictions, pending charges, past failures to turn up, any current supervision or bail, open warrants and any protective order against them. A court may use such a report when it sets the terms of release. Where the charge is a violent crime, the court must use one. The report may not be the only reason to grant or refuse release. Both sides get the results on request. The Oklahoma House passed it 62-23. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 743. It raises the penalty for disturbing a religious service and adds a buffer zone outside. Disturbing a religious meeting stays a misdemeanor. The act sets the penalty at a fine of up to $500, up to a year in county jail, or both. A second or later offense becomes a felony. That carries a fine of up to $1,000, up to two years in prison, or both. The act also changes what counts as disturbing a meeting. Knowingly blocking or hindering a person going in or out is now covered. So is coming within eight feet of someone, without their consent, to hand over a leaflet, show a sign or argue a point. That last rule applies on the public path within 100 feet of an entrance. Two old offenses drop out: putting on a show within a mile, and racing or gambling nearby. The act took effect on the day it was signed. The Oklahoma House passed it 73-21. The Governor signed it.
